utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Yesterday, during the last session, we had an incident, unfortunate situation. I would like to let everybody know that the situation is resolved due to the -- and thanks to the medical care here in The Hague. No reason to worry about it. I forgot yesterday to mention that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. That was decided already last week, on Thursday. We put that on the record that this week, Judge Mindua will not be present and not be able to participate in the hearings due to another commitment. Only Judge Nyambe and myself are the Bench. This is the fact for yesterday, today, and tomorrow's hearing. If there is nothing else, we should continue with the witness. She should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please take your earphones. Good morning and welcome back. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Ms. Palic, welcome back. I have to remind you that the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday still applies. Mr. Elderkin has additional questions for you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to Your Honours and everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Ms. Palic.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, we were just at a point of your story when we finished yesterday talking about the time after the 17th or 18th of July of 1995, when your house had been shelled and you moved up to Stitkov Dol. You said that people moved to Stitkov Dol from the villages on the left-hand side. Could you please explain to us what you mean by that reference, the villages on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about this, I had a picture of my house in my mind. My house was the reference point for left hand and right hand. That means that on the left-hand side there were settlements of Stop, Vrelo. Then there were people of the village of Ljubomislje, Laze, Borovac, who also came to Vrelo, down to Vrelo. Those were the villages that had been occupied at the beginning of the war. Then in 1992 people returned to Ljubomislje to live there, and then in 1995 those inhabitants went in the same direction as me, that is to Stitkov Dol. On the right-hand side there was the centre, the Kula settlement, then Zepa, Slap, Pribicevac, and after that, Ribioc, Vratar, Polje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could please all other microphones be switched off when the witness is speaking. There is a lot of background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Elderkin, this refers to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I see no other microphones are on other than my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How many people were the -- up at Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 2 to 2.500. It's a smaller village, but when you take into account the number of people in those settlements and the total capacity of Stitkov Dol, I would say around 2.500. The fact is that the houses were full those days when we were there. Also, all the auxiliary buildings. There were women with small children, elderly people, disabled. For instance, my mother-in-law was among them. Also, the courtyards and the fields around the houses were full as well. It was maybe a fortunate circumstance that it was summer so people slept in the courtyards and fields. I remember I used to sit with some of those groups. There were pregnant women among them, those who did not find a place in a house to sleep. So they spent the night on meadows.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So just to be very clear, the figure of 2 to 2.500 people is your estimate for the time when you moved up there to escape from the shelling, as did other people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my estimate. I believe that my estimate is very close to the actual number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You've said a little bit about the make-up of the group up at Stitkov Dol so that there were women with small children, elderly people and disabled. Were there also soldiers up at this location when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no soldiers there. There were no able-bodied men there, because this was the most critical period. All the men were at the defence lines. It could have happened that somebody maybe had to look for their family to get the clothes or simply to see their family, but I don't remember anybody except Amir Imamovic. He was the president of the civilian protection of the Zepa municipality. He was also captured later on. He used to come on several occasions. I spoke to him. And also Hamdija Torlak used to come. He was a president of some sort of a board in Zepa and also one of the negotiators before Zepa. So they are the only able-bodied men that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You've mentioned Messrs. Imamovic and Torlak, and also you spoke about negotiations. What was your awareness of negotiations that were taking place with the Bosnian Serb side at that time?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the Serbs imposed certain conditions for the surrender, as well as us leaving the territory. They said that all the men had to surrender and go to collection centres. That's how they used to call them. I would say that they were camps. To put it simply, it was clear that we had to leave Zepa. The Zepa delegation, the negotiators who negotiated on behalf of the authorities of Zepa and the people in Zepa, they tried to get some guarantees for the safety of civilians. I also know that my husband was trying to buy time so that it wouldn't happen that Serb army would march into Zepa and do what they did in Srebrenica, the massacre that they did in Srebrenica. He wanted the international community to realise what happened in Srebrenica and to have enough time in order to do something more humane, in order to prevent a new massacre. And those precisely were the reasons because of which the men in Zepa made superhuman efforts in order to maintain the territory in Zepa until they could negotiate a safe passage of civilians out of Zepa. I remember something that I'm never going to forget. We were already in Stitkov Dol. Hamdija Torlak was one of the negotiators. He came there one evening, to the house where I was with my babies. He came in, and he lied on the floor, silent. Those of us all around him simply waited for him to speak. After some time, he made a deep sigh, and he said, "I had to sign the surrender of Zepa." You could hear it in his voice. It was the voice of a traitor. Of course, we all knew that anybody else who would have found themselves in his position, they would have had to do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was your husband doing during the time while you were in Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I already mentioned this. When Srebrenica fell and the chaos ensued in Zepa, the first thing that my husband requested from the Ukrainian Battalion in Zepa was to protect us. It was clear that they were a small unit and that they could not protect the whole territory. That's why he insisted that they should alert the UN headquarters. He wanted that they should ask Mr. Smith, Mr. Rupert Smith, to provide protection and whatever mechanism that the UN was duty-bound to provide for the enclave. However, this didn't happen. The Ukrainian commander, Dudnjik, went over to check-point 1 where Mladic arrived with his staff. It means that they had occupied check-point 1. It was an UNPROFOR check-point. And the Ukrainian -- the Ukrainian commander was trying, or at least that's what he said to Avdo, that he was trying to request the end of the shelling and the end of the operations around Zepa, and this Ukrainian commander went away one day and never came back. We heard that he was stopped by Mladic. The officer that deputised for him in Zepa said, "Avdo, here's your weapons. This is it." And then my husband and all other who were able to do that went up to the defence lines. It could have been the 13th or the 14th of July, a few days after the fall of Srebrenica. So they were trying to stop the breakthrough of the Serbian Army into Zepa. And this went on until the 24th of July. All this time my husband was with the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You mentioned the Ukrainian commander Dudnjik going to check-point 1. Do you remember the location of that check-point? We know, for example, there was a check-point which the UN numbered 2 but which was at Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the check-point. I thought it was number 1, is the check-point at Boksanica. It was the first check-point when you enter Zepa coming from Rogatica through Borike towards Zepa. That was the first check-point. I thought it was check-point 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, it's just a reminder, you should try to avoid leading questions. Your last one was some sort of leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Indeed, and I'll do my best to avoid that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, during the time you were up at Stitkov Dol, was there any shelling?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was shelling. Stitkov Dol is situated in a particular way. It doesn't mean that it wasn't within the range, but the deployment of the artillery was such that shells did not land into the centre of the village. The shells landed on the other side of the hill that protected the village, and everything around was shelled. During that time, I cannot remember one single moment that the shelling was not going on, but the shells were not landing in Stitkov Dol.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Until when did you stay up there at Stitkov Dol?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained in Stitkov Dol until the 23rd, the evening, the 24th. So we left in the night between the 23rd and the 24th July, sometime after midnight, probably around 2.00 a.m. We waited for the shelling to die down. We had to leave - how should I call it? - this oasis and set out for the mountain. We were in danger. We were threatened by the shelling and by those PAMs and PATs. So we set out at the time when it felt most secure. We assumed that Serbian soldiers would be asleep at that time. That's when we set out for the mountain, and we reached the mountain sometime in the morning of the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how long did you spend at that location, at the mountain?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we arrived in this sort of mountain lodge that belonged to a relative of mine, I went in with the babies. I had to feed them. And then a boy arrived and said that Avdo requested that we should go back, that the evacuation of civilians from Zepa had been agreed. So maybe I stayed there for a couple of hours. Only as long as it took us to simply prepare for the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you moved back down towards Zepa, how many people went with you?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same column. Everybody who went with me also returned and went back. This was a huge column. So all those people who went one way also went back. Also, the news was then transmitted to other groups of refugees, and those people also began to go back towards Zepa, towards the centre of Zepa. They were coming from all sides, from all the places where the refugee groups were. They received this information, and they began to return to Zepa. Now, later on I had the opportunity to speak to some people. Some of them set out immediately, some of them were still afraid, which is perfectly normal. Everybody was afraid to be the first one to leave. They were wondering what was going to happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When did you arrive back in Zepa town?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the early afternoon. Maybe around 2.00, 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you please describe the scene when you arrived into the town.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is the following: It was a very warm day in July. People were coming from all sides carrying bundles, clothes, bags. They were out of their mind. Everybody had lost someone. Everybody were -- was asking about someone. As I have already said, everybody, and especially the people who had been expelled and then ended up in Zepa, had their families divided between Srebrenica and Zepa. Part of the family lived in Srebrenica, and a part of the family in Zepa. Then when the attack on Zepa began, some of them fled towards the mountains, some of them stayed in the woods or in the cave. There was panic. Everybody was asking, "Did you see this one? Did you see that one? Do you know anything about this one?" Then some news arrived about people who were killed at the lines. It was very chaotic. There's one thing that I remember very well. There was a column of buses lined up along the street leading from UNPROFOR to the health centre, and there were Serbian soldiers there. In front of a local cafe, when I approached that place I saw my husband. He was in front of the cafe, and there was a Serbian officer standing there as well, and there were some soldiers around them. When my husband saw me, he approached me. We greeted each other. Of course, I was panicked. He tried to calm me down. He told me that a convoy with wounded people had already left. There were many wounded. I was only worried about him. Of course, I was also afraid, and I was thinking How are we going to cross all that territory? Avdo told me not to be nervous, that everybody would be okay. He told me that Zdravko Tolimir was there. He pointed at that man, and he told me that he agreed with him that he was going to accompany the convoy in his automobile in front of all the buses. He told him to keep his personal firearm and that if he notices anything suspicious, he should just shoot him in the head on the spot. I told him not to believe him. It is true that he looks rather civilised compared to all the creatures around him, but I told him not to trust that man. My husband, of course, tried to be calm. I'm sure that he himself was very well aware of everything. He knew that he could not maintain Zepa. The UN was doing nothing, so he simply had no other choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you see any representatives in Zepa town that day from the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I know that my husband's position was something that he insisted upon when talking to any civilian authorities' representatives who attended negotiations. He insisted that the evacuation process should not go in any other way except with the assistance of the Red Cross, meaning that those who were departing had to be registered and had to be provided safe passage out of the territory where we were being driven out of. However, I didn't see anyone. No one was making any lists or asking us anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were there other soldiers from the Armija of Bosnia and Herzegovina around in the area of Zepa town when you were down there around the time you've described, when you saw your husband?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no ABiH soldiers there. Some lines had fallen. Those people, as throughout the war, tried to reach the Zepa mountain just like we all used to. I suppose that a part of those men withdrew towards it. In Zepa itself, the only able-bodied men were from the civilian authorities, as well as Avdo's driver, Mujo Bicic, and those lightly wounded who were in the hospital. That's all the men that were there. In any case, I can distinctly recall Mujo Bicic and Mehmed Hajric being there. As for any other men, I don't think the Serb army would have allowed it. They simply could not show themselves there. There were Serb soldiers there, however. As one enters Zepa, and when I say that, I have in mind the source of the Zepa River down to the centre of town, all along that route there were groups of Serb soldiers. I remember them so well. They had long beards. They looked unnatural, in a way, for human beings. Their shirts were unbuttoned. They had knives tucked in their belts, and they kept insulting us, throwing remarks at us. They kept saying, "Turks, go to Turkey. Kurds, leave." And they were singing a song about Zepa. However, it was a pejorative song of the population of Zepa heroically defending their hearths, where at the same moment we were being forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what did you do after speaking to your husband, as you described?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I came to terms with what my husband instructed me to do. I got on the bus he pointed out. Still, I refused to believe that the evacuation would be safe. My sister was a girl at the time. I handed one of my babies to her. And I was afraid of how things would develop. For as long as one stayed in Zepa, there was some dignity left, but my worst fear had always been to fall into their hands. When I say "their," I mean the Serb army. Many of them were acquaintances and even friends of mine who, to my great disappointment, became criminals. If things developed in a way that we would be taken off buses, I was afraid to face the same fate as many women who had been taken prisoner in 1992 in Rogatica. They ended up in Zepa after an exchange, previously having gone through different kinds of torture, mainly rape. I also didn't want to see my children suffer. So in a way, we were trying to come up with the best option, and perhaps that was my attempt to hand over one of the babies to my sister so as to give an impression that she was an adult woman. We split afterwards. My mother was there as well, who had been handicapped ever since World War II. We brought her into the bus. In any case, I followed Avdo's instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How many people were there on the bus that you boarded?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus was full. I don't know how many people exactly could fit in, some 50 plus. Some were seated on the floor as well. All the buses were packed. There were a few steps at the back of the bus near the rear door just in front of the last row of seats and there were people sitting there as well, then next to the driver, my mother was seated. In any case, the buses were full.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When did that bus eventually leave from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The boarding process took forever. The people were beside themselves. In any case, we set off sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you know what the intended destination was at the time you set off in the bus?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that we were going towards Kladanj, which was in ABiH territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: On the journey towards Kladanj, did you stop anywhere along the way?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My fear was that we would be taken out of Zepa and then arrested. As we were leaving Zepa, it almost became part of reality, because after we entered Borike -- actually, there is -- there is an open stretch just in front of the stables at Borike, and I could still see the passenger vehicle where Avdo was with Tolimir at the head of the column. Suddenly I got afraid, wondering why we stopped. I was two rows behind the driver. In front of me there were a girl and her mother. I was trying to see up front what was going on. The bus in front of us started again, but we remained in the same place. That bus went ahead and then started backing up into the stables compound. I was wondering why. Before the war, it used to be a horse farm. I couldn't figure out why we were to go there. I had a sudden attack of panic which I had to handle by myself. A soldier came on the bus, who was maybe 25 years old. He leaned his weapon against a railing near the door and began talking to the driver, although I don't know about what. I felt sick, and they gave me some water. I was afraid that we would all be killed and butchered there. However, after a while, the driver said that the bus had a flat tyre and that they backed into the farm to fix it. Indeed, some half an hour later, we set off again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you see your husband again at any point during that journey?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went through Rogatica. What remains etched in my memory is that the Rogatica inhabitants were all lined up along their -- in their windows. Those were our Serb neighbours who came out to see us being driven out. We went through Rogatica and left the town when the buses stopped again. It was already getting dark. I could see my husband in the headlights of the bus, and I was wondering why he was returning. He came onto the bus and remained with us from that spot all the way to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you talk with your husband at all during that journey?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We did talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did he say anything about the situation that you'd found yourselves in?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't discuss that. I kept begging him to take care of himself, telling him that he mustn't trust Tolimir. I asked him to promise that once he got back, he would get away from them. I told him that he should have himself in mind and that he couldn't save anyone unless he saved himself first. I was trying to persuade him to think of his own safety. However, he clearly put it to me that he cannot allow for the civilians to be hurt. He literally said, "Esma, I'll do this job all the way to the end, no matter what happens to me." That was the sort of person he was. He thought he was responsible for those people, and he never even thought of placing himself before anyone else. We also discussed some future plans of ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, whenever you need a break, let us know, please. May we continue, or do you need a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, we should have a break, and I would kindly ask the court usher to inform us when we can continue. We adjourn. --- Break taken at 9.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, I'm glad to see that we can continue, but please let us know at any point in time if you need another break. Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, we've heard about your bus journey the day you left Zepa. Where did the bus finally stop?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stopped when we were told that we have arrived at the separation lines near Kladanj. If -- well, at 9.00 in the morning, we were in that meadow where a UNHCR unit awaited us with refreshments. We walked for a long time before that through a gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where was the last point at which you were still with your husband?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived and got off the buses, my husband and I bid farewell. I was holding one of our daughters in my arms. I told him to take care of himself and left. He told me to stick to the middle of the road. I didn't understand exactly what it meant at the time. Later on, I found out that there were mines along the road. That is why he cautioned me. Let me tell you this as well: That was the road that the people from Srebrenica tried to use to reach the free territory. It was a stretch of about 10 kilometres. Even if they were able to reach that point in attempts to cross the road, they frequently stepped on mines and were killed or wounded. In any case, straying from the road would have been a great risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were your mother and your sister still with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. My grandmother was there as well. I believe I told you that she was handicapped due to World War II. There were other people with us as well, other refugees. It was very difficult. You can carry a child, but what do you do with an elderly person who was over 70 years old? We finally placed her on a branch and pulled her along the road. The entire situation was rather humiliating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you want to leave Zepa when you went down to the town and were prepared to get on the buses? Was that your choice?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't the choice of anyone. It was Ratko Mladic's decision and the decision of his associates, the apparatus he surrounded himself with, including Mr. Tolimir, who is present here. They decided about what would happen with us. They decided we had to leave and in what way. All that story of free choice is absurd viewed in those circumstances. Basically, throughout the war we had no choice. I can tell you two things about it since you ask. If someone asked me to stay in Zepa, promising that my husband would be safe, I would stay there for my entire life, although I had not lived there before. I can also tell you that people lived in Zepa for generations, and such families never dreamt of leaving. They were the true indigenous population of Zepa who never pondered leaving their property. However, they had to leave. They never managed to adapt to the new social circumstances, but they had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were the alternatives for you and for those people if they had stayed, had not got on buses that day?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suffice it to say that Zepa, a small town, was attacked by such a force comprising that many brigades with that much equipment, with so many criminals, most of whom were convicted criminals. One needs to wonder what would have happened with us had we stayed. We simply would not have been allowed to live in a territory which they wanted to see as an ethnically pure Serb area. We surely would have been killed and tortured. We would be no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to buildings in Zepa after the population left in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before I left Zepa, I could see some of the villages in the hills that had been entered by the Serb soldiers. I could see houses ablaze already. They started setting fire to them, and I could see tendrils of smoke. They even torched my parents' house, or whatever was left of it. They razed, torched. Once we left Zepa the last civilian convoy remained as well as a number of wounded who were taken off that convoy in Rogatica as POWs, including some of my relatives. They spent some time in a camp in Rogatica. Then they were taken to Zepa to gather plums and do some work for the Serb army and their leadership, and they knew that at the time that everything was razed to the ground, torched and destroyed; they could see it for themselves. They knew it was all destroyed and anything that could burn was burned. By the time I left, it was no longer a township. It was a jungle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If could we see Exhibit P2178 on the screen, and at page 6, please, of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this is coming up, I would like to ask you something, Ms. Palic. You told us about the situation at the separation line near Kladanj, and your husband left, and you went with your family along the road. Why did your husband not come with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish he had, but then my husband couldn't stand having left the people of Zepa behind. He may have had an opportunity to leave. And I asked myself that question, too, and I thought about it, but if he had left Zepa, if he had left all his troops behind, all those people with whom he had defended Zepa so many times, the people who trusted him and their families, according to his moral criteria and mine, it would have been unbearable for him to leave those friends and associates behind with their families and children to save himself and his own family. It was very difficult to bear for me for years, but today my view is that one's honour comes above all, all other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where did he go from that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He returned with Tolimir, and I asked Avdo, because I was extremely scared, while he was with us, while there were so many of us on the bus, so many civilians -- it seemed to me that he was safer while I could see him, and I was afraid what would happen to him when he returned with Tolimir. My husband tried to convince me that Zdravko Tolimir was a trained officer, and when he said that, he meant that being a trained officer meant honouring the conventions and humanitarian law. And I replied to him, "Well, if he's that highly trained, what's he doing in Zepa?" I knew that Avdo's intention was to convince me and to achieve that I don't torture myself, but it was important to me that Avdo returned safely, and I asked him to give me notice that he had -- that he was safe. And indeed, when I was in Visoko two days later, I got a message from my husband through a ham radio network that he had made it to Zepa safely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When you were travelling on the bus with this group of people from Zepa and with your husband, where was Mr. Tolimir? Was he also on the bus or in a separate car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I suppose that he remained in the front seat of his car. He was not with us. He was probably in his car, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, actually, for the exhibit on the screen, if we could go back to page 5 first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, do you recognise this location that we see in an aerial photograph on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And just for orientation, there's a location indicated with an English worded tag saying "Central Mosque," which is inside a large square on the screen. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this shows the scene as the image was taken on the 27th of July of 1995 with buildings standing in the centre of Zepa village. Does this correspond with the buildings that were there when you were leaving on the 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It mostly does. What -- what I see in the centre, yes. I did -- I didn't see those buildings such as the factory and so on, but the mosque, the cafes, the medical centre, yes, that was all there when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Does this image cover the area where your family's house was located?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly does. My house is on the right side, 150 metres roughly down the main street, to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask for the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: It may help us just to put a marking to indicate where your house was located roughly.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And where we see the other smaller squares on this image running alongside the roads, are those houses as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which roads?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Starting off with the road where you've indicated your family's house. So heading up from there towards the top right of the screen we see some other squares and --

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And how about those heading from where we see the mosque, heading towards the left of the screen, and there's a road that curves up and back down again, and there are some squares along there. Do you know if those were houses?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, both houses, and there was a school, and to the left from the mosque there was the UN base. It was the Ukrainian Battalion. And up there, there was also a neighbourhood called Kula, and the road went on to some surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move away from the microphone. She's chafing the microphone with her clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you help, please, the witness to have a certain distance from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Those are the only markings I'd like to see on this page of the exhibit, and I'd ask if that could be admitted as an exhibit marked in court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This aerial photograph with the markings will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit Number P2178, map number 5, shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2192. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now could we see the next page, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, the central mosque in this picture and the houses on the road running leftwards, the road that first curves up and then down in the picture, can you look at those areas and tell us if you know anything about the destruction of buildings, including the mosque and houses in that area after you had left Zepa in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there when they destroyed these houses and the mosque. The mosque was there on the 27th of July when the last convoy of civilians was blocked in Zepa. They spent the last night in the harem of that mosque. These buildings were burnt down after the civilians had left. It was a part of the process of ethnic cleansing in Zepa. What I do know, and I returned to Zepa after eight years for the first time, and it was in 2003 or 2002 when people first started to go to Zepa. And all houses were destroyed. Some neighbourhoods were completely erased. Vegetation in Zepa is very rich, and everything was already overgrown. It had all become a desert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I don't need to have that image up on the screen any more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, I'm going ask you a few more questions now, and these do concern your husband, and please do indicate to me if you need to take a break at some point. You've mentioned getting news that your husband had returned safely to Zepa after you had arrived in free territory, and you received such a message. Did you hear anything about his whereabouts in the days after that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. That was the only information I got from my husband, and I received it indirectly. On the 28th, in the evening, I heard the news on the radio that the entire civilian population had been evacuated from Zepa, and the whole leadership along with the commander of Zepa, Avdo Palic, had been taken prisoner. That was the moment when my war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Since you heard that your husband had been taken prisoner, did you receive any information that he was then at some point registered by the International Red Cross following his capture?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was at Visoko, I immediately tried to alarm some acquaintances and family who were in Sarajevo and who were closer to the UN and the Presidency to do everything possible to save my husband. There were rules according to which you couldn't immediately report a person missing to the Red Cross. Although there was a war, they adhered to that rule. I did have information that my husband was in Rogatica, though, that they were questioning him there, and I got that information from a Ukrainian soldier, indirectly, that is, and nothing else. And when the conditions were met, I reported my husband missing to -- I reported that to the Red Cross. And when the Red Cross raised that issue at meetings with the Serb side, concerning my husband, they were always saying that they had no idea. It's a long story. At first they even refused to acknowledge they had arrested him. They were saying that they had never heard of him. In a reply that was recorded by the Red Cross, Ratko Mladic said that Avdo Palic had fled through the woods and probably died in the process. And there was a series of lies and invectives. I was unable to learn the truth of my husband. Only in 1996, after the Dayton Accord was signed in the month of January, Abdurahman Malkic and Sado Ramic, two prisoners who were taken prisoner when -- while they were fleeing from Srebrenica, and they spent some time in Bijeljina, in a building where there was a secret prison. There are four cells in that building, in the basement. In one cell there was Abdurahman, in the other there was Sado and in the third there was my husband. When these two were exchanged, they told me that they had seen my husband and that he had stayed there when they were transferred to the Batkovic prison on the 10th of August. No, Avdo was brought on the 10th of August, and they were transferred from that prison, whereas Avdo had to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any letter from your husband after he was captured?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Have you seen or heard from your husband since you got off the bus that took you away from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only got that message that he arrived at Zepa safely and that information from those witnesses. I had no other contact with my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You now know that your husband lost his life.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How many years passed before you learned that he was dead?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fourteen years, that is, in 2009, they identified the remains of my husband. He was found in a mass grave near Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what has been the impact on you and your family of these events, including the disappearance of your husband?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the meaning of everything has changed. Nothing of what I had craved in life but did not achieve was due to the fact that somebody else had made decisions about my life. Since 1992, for the most part, my life was reduced to what Mladic had decided and all that machinery of the Serb forces and political circles that wanted to cleanse those areas from the Muslim population. My life was changed, and the lives of my children too. They didn't have the life that they would have had if their father hadn't died. I lived in agony for 14 years. I wanted to find his mortal remains. Now I'm trying to find those responsible for his murder. So basically ever since the war my life has consisted in the quest for justice, and that has also affected my health.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, thank you very much. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Palic, you know that now Mr. Tolimir has the right to put questions to you during his cross-examination, but let me tell you again, whenever you need a break, please tell us. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I once again send my regards to everyone present including Ms. Palic and may God's will be done in these proceedings and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Palic, since you and I speak the same language, please make a pause so that what you or I say can be recorded. I will try to remind you what you said. On page 24, that is a short while ago, you were asked by the Prosecutor when you learned that your husband was killed, and you said in 2009, after 14 years - that is under line 11 - when he was identified in a mass grave. Here's my question: Do you know, were any other persons killed together with your husband at the same time since they were buried in a mass grave? That may have been a source of information for you looking for your husband and trying to find the perpetrators of his murder. Now, once the cursor stops, please begin your answer. Thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that grave, the bodies of Mehmed Hajric, Amir Imamovic, one Hamdija Dedic. In all, nine bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, were you able to find out whether Mehmed Hajric was killed at the same time as your husband, and was Amir Imamovic killed at the same time as your husband, and is that why they were buried in a mass grave? Please start your answer once this is recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that is a question I would like to put to you. As early as 1998, I found your telephone number, and I wanted to ask you about the fate of my husband, and I did call a number in Banja Luka, but nobody answered the phone. It wasn't easy for me to do, because I knew you wouldn't answer me, and I didn't want to provoke, but all my letters, all my phone calls, all my attempts to learn the truth, which went as far as trying to set up contact with you, I don't know when these individuals were killed, but what I do know is that my husband remained in that secret prison, Vanekov Mlin in Bijeljina after these two persons, Abdurahman Malkic and the other. At first it was by my private efforts that I managed to obtain some information, and later on a statement was taken from the prison warden and he confirmed that Avdo, indeed, was in that secret prison. And in the night between the 4th and the 5th of September, around midnight, Dragomir Pecanac arrived with his driver, and as the warden said, he took over the prisoner. What followed was that Pecanac, in his statement, said that he had handed over Avdo to Colonel Jovo Maric, the commander of some air force unit, a man who at that time was dead already, so he could neither confirm nor deny that allegation, so that all the information about what happened to my husband once he was taken away by Pecanac is insufficient. I don't know what happened to him except that he ended up in that mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic. I know that you wanted to gather as much information as possible. I know that there were some proceedings before national courts. There were some witnesses here who also testified about what you are talking about. However, right now it is most important for you and me and the Trial Chamber to get as many facts about the circumstances of his disappearance as possible. That's why I'm asking you whether you know if he was killed at the same time with others or not. That's very important, because there were many misinformations on the part of the exhumation commission and on the part of those who took part in everything. Because if we don't find out things at this Tribunal, how are we going to find them out? That's why I want you to tell these things to me and to the Trial Chamber. Don't be afraid even if you say something about me. The Trial Chamber should hear everything.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not afraid of the truth. I'm very much for the truth. I just don't know, though, those things. However, the fact is that nobody saw my husband in Rogatica except you, Ljubisa Beara, and other people from Mladic's staff, Pecanac and others. So he was first kept for 15 days there. After that he was taken to Bijeljina, to the secret prison. No other prisoner was with my husband in the cell. They saw him in Bijeljina, but in Rogatica he wasn't seen by any of the other prisoners. You know very well that in Rogatica he was kept in a private apartment. You interrogated him there. Beara interrogated him there.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, weren't you the officer who negotiated with Avdo in Zepa, the officer who was present when Avdo was arrested, when he was kidnapped by the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska in the UN base? In one of the statements we can see that you were present when Avdo was brought there as a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A witness testified here. He was the one who took over Avdo Palic from the persons who arrested him, and he testified about the circumstances. I would like you to only speak about what you saw or what you know, because many people talk many things. You said Maric said this, and then Tolimir saw him and things like that, but I would like you to tell us exactly what you know. That's the only way we can find the truth. I mean, there's no problem if I'm involved in all this.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But isn't that a shame?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I don't know what a shame is. I don't think that it's a shame if you speak the truth, that's why I want you to tell the truth. Could you please answer my following question: You asked me a number of questions here, and I have to tell you that before this Court I only have the right to ask questions and not to answer. So through my questions, I'm going to try to tell you everything I know. I'm going to say everything that I can say, everything that I am allowed to say. Please tell us, do you know that at the time while your husband was interrogated in that apartment, he was interrogated by the State Security Service and not the army? You said that he was in that mill.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was four.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And do you know that he was also interrogated there by the same organs?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't registered. There is no trace of him being registered anywhere except one thing. The only trace comes from the fact that the warden of the prison in Vanekov Mlin was sufficiently intelligent, and he requested that Pecanac should sign a certificate certifying that he took over the prisoner. So this is the only trace from which we can see that Avdo was treated as a war prisoner, because he was handed over as a war prisoner. So that's one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I need to ask if we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, you told us about the commissions set up by the government and Republika Srpska. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as I was saying, none of those commissions managed to yield the answer, which was the basic reason for the establishment of the commissions. They did not investigate those responsible, and they did not tell me where the body of my husband was. You are now referring me back to the institutions in Sarajevo. Look, I do not amnesty anybody in this case, but the fact remains that I did not expect to receive an answer from them. All this could have happened the way that it did happen. When we requested them to identify possible mortal remains it was one thing, but in this particular case all the responsibility rested with the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic. Please tell the Trial Chamber who identified your husband. Tell us everything you know about that so we can see whether they found him in the mass grave or whether they placed him in the mass grave after the identification, because this is going to reveal many things about the manner in which those people were killed.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2009, I received information that my husband had been identified. That was a great shock for me. Why? Because I was informed that the body that was found out to belong to my husband had been buried in Visoko as an unidentified body, that it had been exhumed from a mass grave in Vragolovi close to Rogatica in 2001, and the identification was done by the ICMP, because they do all the identifications in the former Yugoslavia. That's an international institute for the DNA analysis. So the body of my husband was exhumed from a mass grave in 2001. It was transferred to Visoko. This means that it was handed over to the federal commission. Since no identification was made, because at the time they did not do DNA analysis, he was buried as an unidentified body. You have to understand that this was a great frustration for me. I passed by that graveyard on many occasions, and I didn't know that the body of my husband was lying there. I consider the Government of Republika Srpska responsible, because if they told me that they told the truth I would have known in the body of my husband was there. We could have done all this analysis before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic. Now, based on all your knowledge, could you answer my following question: Do you maybe know whether the mortal remains of your husband were found in an individual grave or in a common grave with other people who were killed at different times and different places?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they were all killed in the same place. My husband's body was found in the mass grave near Rogatica where there were also the bodies of Mehmed Hajric, Amir Imamovic and Hamdija Dedic, as well as six other victims. It is certain that the three I mentioned were killed in the area of Rogatica. Actually, there is information to that extent, including information on the perpetrator. However, I don't know where my husband had been. This is what I'm trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to point out a key fact, which is whether he was killed at the same time, so that to be buried in the same grave, or was he exhumed and then subsequently put in it. This is what you need to research, because it will provide many answers ultimately.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is indicia in existence that this was a secondary grave. However, as I said, they're only indicia. I think you know that better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since say that there are indications that it was a secondary grave, are there also indications that someone buried people killed in different places in that single grave in order to cover up any traces and lead the investigation in a wrong direction?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If anyone did that, it was done by members of the VRS in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also said that Republika Srpska was to blame. Could the VRS bury the mortal remains of your husband and others in Visoko, those allegedly found in the mass grave, because it is in federation territory.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an ugly question. I'm telling you and the Chamber this: There wasn't a single day spent that I didn't do something trying to find out where my husband was. I have the decision of the war crimes chamber in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a senior judicial body which states that it was the authorities of the RS who are tasked with determining or defining the fate of Avdo Palic. If he is found to be alive, he should be released immediately. If he is dead, the mortal remains need to be returned to the family and perpetrators tried. It means that the mortal remains were to be given to the family, not to any federal commissions, because there are three such commissions, including the government of the RS. But not a single one was able to tell us that he was, say, killed in Rogatica and buried at this particular place. This is the lead we would have followed. Only the last commission hinted at that, and then I insisted that targeted individual identification be done of the bodies in the grave. If the commissions appointed by the RS between 2001 and 2007, had they done their job, everything would have been clear, but where are the results of investigations? Throughout the investigation, I don't see any responsibility with the federation commission. I believe this is imputed. We looked for so many years, we insisted, and all along the body was on our side. It's a classical set-up so as to appear that, yes, it is ultimately you hiding the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. You know that the perpetrator of a crime is trying to cover up tracks. I'm asking you this in goodwill. Please consider it carefully. Did you ask the Prosecution who carried out the exhumation in Vragolovi, The VRS or the commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you find out who it did and who took his body to Visoko and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question you put to me is illogical. As I said, the exhumation of the mass grave in Vragolovi was carried out in 2001, and if I'm not wrong, the VRS no longer existed. There were only the joint armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How could then the army exhume his body? It is a fact that until 2001 he was buried in VRS territory, and exhumations were never carried out by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. Please consider this carefully: These joint organs which carried out exhumations, did they take your husband's body to Visoko, to ABiH territory, and buried him there, or was this done by Republika Srpska, to take his body to the territory of the other entity? This is the question you need to explain to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done by representatives of the federal commission. The rule was -- well, it's difficult and tedious to explain, but every commission had a list of people they were looking for. The RS government is duty-bound to assist with identifying and locating people in their territory, as is the federation in its territory. Of course, many more Muslims went missing, and for the most part searches were done in -- in RS territory. Now it turns out that it's the federal commission to blame, and they found him, and the blame is not on those who killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I didn't raise the issue of the blame. I raised the issue of who found the body in the mass grave and who took it to Visoko. Perhaps you can tell us I know, I don't know or something else. When you say the federal commission, the Court doesn't know which commission it is. Is it the one controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its government or is it some other commission and territory?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we are referring to this, I cannot refer to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the VRS. These two military formations ceased their existence once the Dayton Accords were signed, and shortly afterwards, joint BiH forces were created. I believe you know that. There are no separate armies any more. This is done by commissions for searching for those who went missing, and there are two, one in the RS and the other in the federation. Need I say more?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. I have no further questions about this, because you are putting in the context of who is to blame. I was simply trying to find out whether the federation commission working in the territory of the federation was supposed to go to Rogatica, which is in RS territory. Are they free to come without any authorisation or approval by the RS authorities?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must be permission to come, and there must be police security provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That is why I asked you. How come a body is taken from Rogatica to Visoko, from the RS to the federation, without you knowing and without you being informed?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the ultimate crime, actually. Had I not done what I did, had I not fought, had I not searched, had I not have the decision by the Court ordering the RS authorities to hand over the body to the family -- and I never turned to the federal commission because I didn't think they were responsible. This question was before all other questions. The disappearance of my husband was taken out of the context of those who went missing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I fought for him to be found. I fought for the truth to be learned, and there were court decisions on my side. There's also the fact that my husband was the most senior prisoner in terms of rank on any side, the Croatian, the Serbian, or the army side. It was a well-known case. This is why I believe it to be more of a crime by the RS, because they knew, but they didn't want to deliver despite the obligation by the chamber for human rights and despite the decision of the constitutional commission of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They simply did not provide information that the body of my husband was exhumed, and that was in the territory of the federation. Do you think that anyone in the federation would have an interest in hiding my husband's body? What for?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is not up to me to have an opinion about this. I simply put questions about what you said. You said you passed by the graveyard without knowing. So the person who buried him didn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That somebody is the Government of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Government of the RS bury him in Visoko in federation territory without the federation knowing?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, if I give you something without telling you what it is, how can you be responsible for it? Once the body was exhumed from the grave in Rogatica, did anybody provide a list of those victims, saying this is Mehmed Hajric, Amir Imamovic, Hamdija Dedic, and Avdo Palic? No one said so. It is your responsibility or the responsibility of the person who killed them, the person who located that mass grave there, and it is the responsibility of the Government of the RS who did not conduct an efficient investigation and did not hand over the body in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. You know best how to arrive at the truth. It is up to me to ask you to -- whether you have considered all these elements, and since we entered the realm of politics, you may well end up without appropriate answers on either side. I hope you are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not a question. I think this is a very difficult matter to deal with in this courtroom. I think it's very important for Mr. Tolimir, and it is a very serious matter for you, Ms. Palic. I would like to invite both speakers to calm down, if that is possible, dealing with this problematic matter. We should avoid debating. We should try to continue by putting questions and answer questions. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on and put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am trying to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were asked by Judge Fluegge why your husband did not join you when he arrived with you at the separation line at Kladanj. You described how you arrived there and how he went back. My question is this: When your husband came on your bus, did he tell you that I offered him to go to ABiH territory with you, and it was because of that that I let him to go to your bus to accompany you to the separation line? Did he tell you that as you were moving between the two lines of confrontation?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not. Not in those words. He didn't mention your offer. Somewhere in my memory it seems to linger this idea that you were ready to let him go. He was a hindrance to you in Zepa. Maybe I simply wanted him to come with us. In such circumstances, your only -- only your need for survival operates properly. Avdo was a commander. Furthermore, he was the person who enjoyed the trust of his people. He radiated peace and security, which was important for the inhabitants of Zepa. Had Avdo left, what would have been with the people? Only one convoy had left by that time. I'm certain that Srebrenica would have occurred in Zepa. How would Avdo be able to go on living knowing that he had abandoned his people? Also, what would that have meant in terms of his service? It would surely be seen as a betrayal. By that time, I got used to this underhanded approach of yours as to who started the war, how, when. It's always the same thing over and over again. There's only one thing that is certain: For as long as you are here, you're important in that context. Mr. Tolimir, if you were indeed of such good intentions, why didn't you save my husband once his mission was completed, once he saved the people of Zepa? Instead, you offered to him a dirty way out, a coward's way out. Would you have abandoned your people? I know many would. However, I'm proud.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic and everybody else, it's a very emotional situation for you, of course, but it's up to Mr. Tolimir to put questions to you and not the other way round, because we are in a trial, so that there is no possibility for Mr. Tolimir to answer your questions I suppose you have, and I understand that very well, but it's only for him to put questions to you. Mr. Tolimir, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, apart from taking care of the civilian population, was your husband obliged to take care of his brigade first and foremost, and did he want his brigade to get out of Zepa either by convoy or some other way, and was there resistance to that by the Sarajevo authorities? Do you know anything about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that -- that Avdo only accepted an evacuation of his forces by air, because he didn't want his soldiers to take a land route without Red Cross monitoring. Only by air, for reasons of safety. And as for resistance in Sarajevo, no. I know that there were talks about that in Sarajevo, and there were representatives of the Zepa War Presidency involved, and they did everything to bring about such an evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. Since there was no evacuation of able-bodied men, was it logical for him to try to provide support for their evacuation through direct contacts with the Sarajevo authorities, including Alija Izetbegovic, and did he tell you that he had been offered to leave and do that and contact his unit the same way he contacted you at Visoko?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D55, paragraph 108. It's on page 30. Now Ms. Palic can see what her husband wrote to Alija Izetbegovic concerning the -- concerning his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see the text right below the third paragraph. This is the letter which your husband in his capacity as brigade commander sent to Alija Izetbegovic on the 26th of July. I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you are going to quote, please tell us where we can find the English text. Is it the last paragraph on that page, 29? Yes. Now I see it. Paragraph 108. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote again what Avdo Palic wrote to Alija Izetbegovic on the 26th of July: "President -- Mr. President, at about 2100 hours negotiations at Boksanica at which General Smith, Hamdija Torlak, President of the Executive Board of Zepa, and war criminal Ratko Mladic were present concluded: As General Suvalic informed me today during these negotiations on agreement about the exchanges of all for all accepted also by our side should have been adopted. Minister Muratovic was supposed to be present but he wasn't because security was not guaranteed for him. General Suvalic also informed me about this. During the negotiations General Smith stated that our side did not accept the agreement about the exchange of all for all and that our side was demanding some additional concessions. Hamdija Torlak remained at the place of negotiations in Boksanica and he was told that if we were ready for an exchange of all for all during the night until 0800 in the morning, General Smith would let us know so that a plan of helicopter evacuation could be prepared. "President, I ask you on behalf of my brigade which is on the verge of a nervous breakdown, if our side does not accept the agreement to undertake everything so that it accepts the agreement and free us from our -- from our predicament. We cannot believe that this problem looks like you will not solve it. If the problem's not resolved tomorrow, I must make a decision to make a breakthrough with 2.000 men and 10 -- and a thousand rounds."

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10.000 rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, "10.000 rounds and you have the picture of Srebrenica and intelligence data that we are blocked from all sides. Tomorrow the evacuation of civilians will be over and UNPROFOR will immediately pull out so that tomorrow we will probably be left to fend for ourselves. "President, I ask you, in the name of the soldiers who have been fighting for the last five days --

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Fifteen days, like lions. I ask you in the names of fallen soldiers, and in my ranks, I have sons or parents of those who died, I ask in the name of the evacuated families and children, who can hardly wait to meet their fathers who are left on Zepa mountain to be slaughtered or annihilated in any other way. I ask you again in the name of my soldiers to make it possible for us to defend Bosnia in some other battle-fields, to liberate it and to die like men. Do not let us die of hunger, of the most common diseases, because we don't have a single doctor but already have sick people who cannot reach the free territory if we start the breakthrough," and so on. And now let's take a look at the last sentence in this paragraph: "He could have left yesterday with the wounded, but did not want to leave his brothers-in-arms. He wanted to know to the end what would be their fate and share it with them. I will be waiting for your reply, hoping that you will successfully resolve this problem." And the ERN number of the document from which this is a quote can be seen in footnote 164. Did you know that your husband sent such appeals to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and that there was no helicopter evacuation in spite of that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after my departure from Zepa, so I can't have known this. What I do know is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was continuous communication and that there were continuous efforts on the part of the Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To inform the Sarajevo authorities of the situation in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is one fact: Nobody, apart from us who were there, including you, Mr. Tolimir, could not have a faithful picture of what was going on there. Avdo did all he could that the Sarajevo authorities get correct information, and the UN in Sarajevo too, that the people be adequately protected. If you're asking me, I can say that it was my -- it is my personal impression that we were left to our own resources and that everybody had left us at the mercy of those -- those thugs that I saw in Zepa, the Serb army. Could the Sarajevo authorities do more? I don't know. I know that the UN could have done more. They could have stopped you. And this is the source of my bitterness. But that does not justify what you did there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. I kindly ask you the following: Your husband wrote this one day after your departure. The situation did not change in that one day. And the date before your departure agreement D51 was signed. Could we please see it in e-court. Did your husband talk to you, and did you know that an agreement was signed under which the soldiers were also supposed to cross over to BH Army controlled territory under certain conditions? Did he tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that they would come, too, because otherwise I wouldn't have left him if I hadn't hoped that he would join me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you that he spoke to me in the car about the evacuation of able-bodied men and that we had the idea of him to go to federation territory and arrange the evacuation from Zepa by helicopter, irrespective of the pride that matters to all of us there? But if we look at the result of that pride, that's something else.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me, and it's normal he didn't, because then I would have tried much harder to persuade him to come with us. But I repeat that this was a cowardly ruse. Let us think about the objective situation where you give an opportunity for the number one man to leave. What else can that be called but betrayal?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. That's your opinion. But those who had to resolve problems in the war such as your husband and I, had to find some -- had to find agreement. Now we can see here an agreement on the disarmament of the able-bodied population in the Zepa enclave. And the other problems are outlined in these ten items. Please take a look at item 2, which says: "Avdo Palic shall issue an order to his troop -- troops to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The civilian and able-bodied population --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] of Zepa shall assemble around the UNPROFOR base in Zepa which shall be assigned to the army of RS, that the units under the command of Avdo Palic have accepted the truth and will not try to take advantage of it." Now look at item 10. It reads: "UNPROFOR, the ICRC, the UNHCR, and other international humanitarian organisations, in co-operation with the Army of Republika Srpska, shall enable the transport of its civilian population from Zepa to territory under the control of Rasim Delic's army or to third countries of their choice in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949." Which means that, apart from the able bodied and the civilian population, your husband had to tackle the problem of the able bodied who he commanded. Here is my question. Would all able-bodied men have accepted the agreement if your husband had signed it, and if the Sarajevo authorities accepted it? Would that have been a better outcome that would have enabled them to come home to their families as your husband wrote in his letter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will get back to your question, but first I can see whether this says done on the 24th of July. This is the agreement that Hamdija Torlak had to, was forced to, sign, which means that this agreement was imposed by force. That's one thing. Another thing: I state with full responsibility that if it had been agreed for the troops to surrender to you, the Serb army, what would have ensued would have been the same massacre as in Srebrenica. I also don't know what would have happened to the civilians, but the troops would have been massacred. I'm positive about that. You know that even those who fled to Serbia were mistreated, and that in a country which, conditionally speaking, was not at war. And what would have become of them if they had surrendered to those in Zepa? There is no such favourable option as you're trying to present it. If you had been so harmless, you wouldn't have shelled and killed so persistently. You wouldn't have come from the other end of the country to drive us out of there. You are saying that you would have let the Zepa troops to leave without harming them? Oh, come on. Your persistence to conquer in that territory was incredible. You know how much effort was put into conquering Zepa from 1992 to 1995, and yet you're now trying to convince me that you would have let the soldiers to leave and join their families. Well, why didn't you do that at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have stop you. We need our second break now. We're running out of time. But I would like to mention that on page 48, line 19, it reads: "Please look at item 2 which says," and then you were quoting, but that was, in fact, item 3 of the document in front of us. Thank you. We must have our second break now, and we will continue at 12.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mrs. Palic, while we looked at D51 in e-court, you asked whether it said the 24th of July. I have to say yes, it says so at the beginning, in the first paragraph and also at the very end, and the agreement was signed on the 24th of July, 1995. While it is still on the screen, I'm not a good reader, so that's probably the reason why I read the third paragraph instead of the second, but could you now take a look at the seventh paragraph where it says: "In accordance with the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August 1949 and the Additional Protocols of 1977, the civilian population of Zepa shall be given the freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this was signed on the 14th of July, 1995, can you tell us whether you know when the Dayton agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the 14th, the 24th. That's what I asked you, whether it was the 24th. When the Prosecutor was posing questions, I said that I remember it well, that I remember that Hamdija Torlak came in one evening and then lied on the floor in the house where I was with my babies. He was silent for a long time, and then he let out a deep sign and said, "I had to sign the surrender of Zepa." He was a desperate man at that moment. Anybody else in the same position could not have done anything else. You were the masters of life and death. That's how you acted, and that's how it was. But whoever would have been in the same situation would also feel the same burden of treason. That's why he had a very hard time. So everything that you see written here, everything written here was written on the instructions of Ratko Mladic, and this document was probably written just for the purpose of writing it, not for the purpose of actually agreeing on something.
