So what I see here in this document is for me yet another proof of the fact that you defined the rules of the game, that you had your own goals and your own visions. You mention Geneva Conventions here, but you cared nothing for them. This document is yet another proof that you blackmailed the negotiators from Zepa. And as for the Dayton agreement it was signed on the 14th of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't see what it has to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It has to do with this, please. Does that mean that this agreement was in force for less than 6 months and after that everybody had the right to return to the territory from which they fled during the war. Isn't that something that this agreement guarantees? And aren't some people living in Zepa now? You yourself said that you went to Zepa after the war. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question is extremely provocative, but as I told you, I am used to the ruses generated by the machinery of the Serbian nationalism. The Dayton peace agreement guarantees a lot of things, things that were never implemented, never ever. On the contrary. As for the return to Zepa, it began probably sometime in 2001. I would like to inform the Chamber and remind you in July 1995, when you arrested Avdo, you know that the army was disintegrating, that whatever choice they would have been offered, they were afraid and they couldn't make proper decisions. That's why it was agreed that the men should be -- should cross over to Serbia. A number of able-bodied men who were in Zepa crossed the Drina River, arrived to Serbia and were then accommodated in collection centres Sljivovica and Mitrovo Polje, I think. Those men were later taken to third countries, America, Norway, Scandinavian countries, Australia. They were scattered all over the world. Then they invited their families to join them, and they started new life in those foreign countries. So what am I trying to say here? You imposed conditions that those men could not return to Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that they went to third countries instead. When they went abroad and when they started their new lives, well, who would return to Zepa then?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one more thing. Where were they supposed to come back? I want to remind you that if you look at the big house that belonged to my parents, together with auxiliary buildings and other things, it was a large property. Today there is only a small weekend house consisting of two rooms. And there are many similar houses in Zepa. This is the so-called process of rebuilding. There is nothing in Zepa. There are no factories. There are no jobs. There is nothing in Zepa. And when you were chasing us away, you knew very well how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic. Could I ask you to make your answers slightly shorter so that I can manage to finish this cross-examination. Now, as for the events, there was a witness yesterday who testified about crossing over to Serbia. You said that it was agreed that they would cross to Serbia. Do you know who agreed that, where and how?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Milosevic expressed the willingness to accept the men from Zepa under the auspices of UN and I assume the Sarajevo authorities. Nobody from Zepa was involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So if it was done under the auspices of the UNHCR and the Sarajevo authorities, does that mean that the Serbs took those people to Australia? Ah, yesterday's witness said that he returned after three months. Were they able to return whenever they wished to return?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did he return after three months? After -- no. To Zepa? Nobody returned to Zepa before 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic. You have to bear in mind that we had a witness here whose job is to issue permits for the return to Zepa, and he said that he personally issued 300 such permits which enabled people to return to Zepa. I think that we should speak only about things that we know about, and we should be more brief. Do you happen to know that more than 300 families returned to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it was that many. A number of them returned, but not that many. But the return did not start prior to 2001. People couldn't dream about going back to Zepa then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. People returned whenever they wanted, as you yourself said. But tell me this: Does this agreement enable everybody to come back after the hostilities? Is that ethnic cleansing? If the agreement says that people can come back after the hostilities, and if that is also something envisioned by the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Dayton agreement created the possibility for that, but the Serbian authorities did not create such responsibility. In Zepa they did not create jobs. They didn't give us the school. They didn't give us the electricity. They didn't give us the most elementary conditions for life. There are things on a declaratory level and then there are things in reality. As for the Serbian authorities, the Dayton agreement is always declaratory when it suits them but in actual fact it has an actual effect only when it suits them as well. Also, you yourself in this agreement mentioned a number of things only on the declaratory level, but in real life, there was no return because there were no conditions fit for life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I stopped you because you were overlapping again. Please wait with your next question until the translation has finished. Now, again your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mrs. Palic, please tell us, this agreement signed by the representatives of the Muslim and Serb side, does it allow for the return of people after the hostilities? Take the last sentence in item number 7. Take a look at the last sentence in item number 7.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to this document, that's what's written in it, but I have to say it once again, this is a document dictated by Ratko Mladic. He used it for his own purposes. The influence on the contents of this document was not in the hands of Hamdija Torlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday at page 4, line 14 -- or more generally, on page 4, line 14 onwards, you spoke about Hamdija Torlak. First you said that your husband was trying to buy time through negotiations, that that was the reason why he sent the negotiators. Now, that means that he gave them the mandate and instructions. Then, further on you said that Hamdija Torlak arrived in Stitkov Dol. He entered the house, lied on the floor, and remained silent. After some time, he let out a deep sigh, and he said, "I had to sign the agreement. I had to sign the surrender of Zepa." You could feel it in his voice. You could hear the voice of a traitor, although we all knew that that was the situation that could not have been avoided. So I didn't actually intend to ask you this, but since you mentioned it and you emphasise Hamdija Torlak, I have to ask you: Was the agreement signed when you were in Stitkov Dol? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this was not on the transcript of yesterday but of today, just for the sake of the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we see page 7 of today's transcript, lines 19, 21, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mrs. Palic said: "When I arrived to the mountain lodge, a boy arrived and told us that the evacuation of civilians from Zepa had been agreed and that we should prepare ourselves," et cetera. My question is: Did Hamdija Torlak come to Stitkov Dol or to the mountain lodge after the agreement on the evacuation of civilians had been signed? I, of course, allow for the possibility that you made a mistake about the dates, because you weren't very attentive to details at the time.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamdija Torlak came to the house in Stitkov Dol. On that night, we set out for the mountain, and just as we had arrived, that boy came to tell us that we should go back because an evacuation was agreed. Why did they return so quickly? You know that better than me. But the fact is that I heard it with my own ears, that I was present. I heard the man say that he was forced to sign that agreement. Although he didn't want to do it, he said that he had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, on the 24th -- were you in that mountain lodge when the boy arrived to tell you that the agreement had been signed?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume -- yes, yes. It's the 24th, because the evacuation began in the afternoon on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that Hamdija Torlak, lying on the floor, told you that he signed the evacuation or he was silent and didn't want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the night after that he told us that he didn't want to sign it but had to sign it. That was the same night that we set out for the mountain. Now, look, of course I'm quite tired right now and you're trying to break my concentration. We are talking about the dates now. First the 23rd, the 24th in the afternoon we went out. Then it was the 25th, 26th, 27th. I'm talking about the dates that determine the rest of my life. The night before we left Stitkov Dol, you know it was the last night. We went towards the mountain only during the last night, because we didn't know that those conditions would actually be accepted, the conditions that you imposed. Hamdija did sign them, and then I don't know exactly what happened in the morning, and that's when we were told that the evacuation would have been organised. And then when we returned, we thought that we would see some Red Cross vehicles. We thought that this part of evacuation had also been agreed, but I didn't see any such vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. Let us look at a footage from Zepa so that we can actually see the picture, and perhaps that will help you recall things. Do you see this person in the still?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us who it is?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamdija Torlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. He is putting his coat on his shoulders, and he's about to sit at the negotiating table. We need to hear what he says, and perhaps we should start playing from 25:44.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Mr. Torlak said in his first sentence when he mentioned the government and when he said that they agreed that it was best for the entire population to leave Zepa? Did you hear that on the footage?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. But this is the same as the candy Mladic distributed in Srebrenica before the cameras. You were taping Hamdija so that he would be forced to say that we decided to surrender and we decided to leave. Why were you not taping as you were destroying, burning what you did when he came? What was the purpose of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, we need the document number you are using at the moment. You didn't indicate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is P740.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 19th of July, 1995. At 26 minutes, 5 seconds, to 26 minutes, 26 seconds. This is the only part we'll be referring to given the shortness of time. Can we keep playing, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, could you hear Mr. Mladic's first sentence? What did he say he would make possible?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did he say that he would allow a freedom of choice?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. But I need to repeat, this was taped for Mladic's purposes. I repeat, why was Mladic not taped issuing orders to kill, butcher, burn, et cetera? This was recorded for his needs, and you are relying on it now. As for any freedom of choice, since 1992, as of the moment you surrounded Zepa with tanks, we never had any freedom of choice. I need to remind you that what you are trying to do is ironic. You know better than me what your aims and intentions were, and now you're asking me to acknowledge your goodness? You killed. You torched. People went missing. There's nothing you didn't do, and now you're discussing freedom of choice as if we were idiots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. I apologise. We are showing you the footage of a meeting, and Mladic never issued orders such as kill, burn, and slaughter. If you have something to that effect, you need to show it to us, of course. Otherwise, let us continue with the footage, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the wounded leave first from Zepa in keeping with the agreement reached by Mladic, Kulovac, and Torlak, and do you know whether Mr. Kulovac took the wounded out?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. If I can remind you, Dr. Benjamin Kulovac never used to smoke. He did not enjoy that vice. I knew him well. He was a friend of mine. But here you can see he's extremely nervous and that all this is a situation that is well set up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us shows the rest of the footage to Mrs. Palic and she can see if we forced Mr. Kulovac to smoke and whether we staged anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good forbid. I don't even want to hear his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, we should see the footage of the 25th of July. This one was of the 19th of July. From 26 minutes to 26 minutes, 26 seconds. Next we'll see P740, the evacuation on the 25th of July, 1995, that is to say, the day Ms. Palic left Zepa, from 36 minutes 40 seconds to 37 minutes 50 seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The correct reference to the day Ms. Palic left Zepa, I understood from her earlier testimony she left on the 24th of July but Mr. Tolimir has just stated that the evacuation on the 25th was the day she left. If he could confirm the correct day, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, could you please repeat the day of the evacuation and when you left the village of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 24th, in the evening. That is when I left Zepa. That is what I recall, and that is what I made notes of. On the 25th, we were in Kladanj, and during that day we travelled on, eventually reaching Visoko on the 26th. That's in my diary. I may have gone wrong by a day, but I think it was on the 24th. I think this is the footage showing Avdo coming back that day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do not dispute Ms. Palic's words. I just wanted to show the footage of the 25th of July showing the evacuation. And she may well have left on the 24th. I have no issue with that. Can we please play now from 36 minutes, 18 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please. We stopped at 36:45.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see whether these soldiers are away from the bus on the opposite side of the road next to the destroyed building?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But do you know what the distance is? Ten metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now have a look at who's next to the bus at the distance of 1 metre.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's keep playing from 36:45, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recognise your husband in this still, and do you know if he was there during the boarding process on the same day when you were there, or is this another day perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't see myself here. I suppose this was on the day he returned. He was close by. Whenever the people were upset, he was there to help them during the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's keep playing so that Ms. Palic could identify certain people and remind herself of the events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see these two men with sheets of paper in hand, and, if so, can you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised Mehmed Hajric as the person in the white shirt. I didn't recognise the person on the right-hand side though. Mehmed Hajric was the president of the Zepa War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's keep playing from 37 minutes on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Stop, please. We stopped at 37:40.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see the man in uniform with a patch on his right upper arm?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see him, but I don't see the patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did UNPROFOR members wear uniforms similar to this one? Could he have been an UNPROFOR member?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his face. I don't know the man, so you're asking in vain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's keep playing from 37:40.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please, at 37:50. We won't be using the footage any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether Mr. Hajric was conducting the evacuation with the help of UNPROFOR members because we saw one of them with a UN patch, and were they closer to the people than the VRS soldiers who as you said were standing some 10 metres away?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a difference in position, but it all took place within a perimeter of 10 metres. If this was indeed a Ukrainian soldier, between him and your soldiers the distance was 10 metres judging by the footage. You showed the corner of the cafe building where I saw you standing with your soldiers when I arrived in Zepa. At that point in time, the bus was behind the building where the staff was, whereas when I was leaving, the buses were lined along the street between the UNPROFOR base and the hospital. So this is such a small area. This is an attempt to confuse a person who's not familiar with the location itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. Can you tell us whether you know if any lists were made based on which you were put on buses so that it would be ensured that you finally arrived in the territory you were trying to reach, and was this done by the representatives of the Zepa authorities?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one registered me. When I enter the bus, I didn't see anyone making lists. I know that on another convoy on another day that people were listed. Some acquaintances of mine told me, because they were on that convoy. I didn't inquire much. They just told me that lists were made on that convoy. However, there were no lists on our convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that at page 10, lines 10 to 12. Let's look at D173 next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Before we leave from this video. Please keep it. Keep the video on the screen, please. We would like to go back to 37 minutes, 40 seconds, if that is possible. Yes. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: No, actually, I don't have a question. I would just like, if possible, for the video to move to show this individual in uniform completely, a little bit up, because there is this unclear patch. I just want to go up in the position in which he is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation. Perhaps your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please go back from 37:40 to 37:30, and then we'll see the entire frame.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have now seen the arm above this blurred band, and we saw the -- the patch. Could you please continue playing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is fine. We should now continue. You asked for the document D173. It should be, please, placed on the screen. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us display paragraph 16 of this document, which is on page 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is the statement of Mr. Joseph. Have you heard of him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Joseph is a witness. Actually, he understood -- he helped me understand what was happening in Zepa after my departure. Mr. Joseph arrived at Zepa after I had left, I think, because when we spoke once, we concluded that I must have left before he arrived with somebody else from the United Nations. I know the man very well, because I melt him on a couple of occasions when I needed a witness who -- who saw Avdo being arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see what he says in paragraph 16. "We created written lists of the evacuees, and as far as I can recall, we had separate lists for each vehicle. I handed over those lists later either to UNHCR or someone in UNPROFOR. We also tried to place one UNPROFOR soldier to each vehicle, but I'm not sure if we managed to do it all the time during the evacuation." Here's my question: Do you believe that Joseph indeed did that? He also came to testify here, and he was sent to Zepa by General Smith to take part in the evacuation and see to it that everything goes as it should.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you when I was getting on the bus, I saw nobody registering people. I'm not familiar with this type of situation. That's one thing. And another, I have information that some people on the following day, who were part of other convoys, were registered. That's what I learned afterward. Those persons on those convoys were registered, and there were lists of people. And then I think that Mr. Joseph and I weren't there at the same time. This is what we concluded at one point. Whether that's really the case, well, I don't know. I can't go into that now. But any way, I wasn't registered by anybody, but I do have information that some other people were registered who were on subsequent convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's not all that important. Maybe they didn't want to interview you at the time because you were a well-known personality. Maybe that person from the Zepa authorities put your name on a list because they wanted you to arrive in the free territory, and they didn't want to expose you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But where are those lists? Has anybody ever seen them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait. Please wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, please read the second sentence of paragraph 16. It's in the second line. Thank you. It says: "I later handed over those lists either to UNHCR or someone in UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you said that somebody from the Zepa authorities drafted those lists, and now we see that it reads they were handed over to UNPROFOR and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. It really is not my intention to say anything false. We've just seen Hajric. Have you seen him holding a list?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I personally am concerned, you may not be stating false things bluntly, but you are telling the same old story again about the allegedly good intentions of the Serb army. But what were you doing in Zepa in the first place unless you wanted to kill people, burn down the place and destroy it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. Since this is the kind of language you're using, you're forcing to go me show some documents that clearly show what your husband did when it comes to burning and slaughtering. But before that, let me ask you whether you know that the VRS conducted sabotage and terrorist activities against Zepa.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that they did that, but it was so frequent in 1992, 1993, 1995. On a number of occasions they massacred people. And I think I would need quite some time to enumerate these sabotage raids, as you call them where you slaughtered -- well, let me give you one example Brezevo Ravno. They massacred people in their sleep, and there's a series of such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, I don't want to oppose you. Be free to say whatever you want to say. But do you know whether there were sabotage groups from Zepa going into the territory controlled by the VRS? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to make one thing perfectly clear. When you surround a place, encircle it and isolate it, only if everybody there is dead you must -- you can expect that they will not try to find a way out of their situation. It's a fact, and I know, and it happened at least twice in my presence, and I -- I also mentioned it yesterday, but I'll repeat, not only were we isolated without medication, without clothes, footwear, food, the greatest problem was the hunger which reached its peak in late autumn and in winter. People were hungry. I remember two such situations when some men came to Avdo and said, "Let's go attack Borike, because my child is hungry." And others put forward other reasons. People were already fed up with waiting to starve to death or be killed by Kusic's shells. But Avdo didn't let them go on such raids. And it wasn't Kusic who saved Borike and Han Pijesak and the other places in the surroundings. It was Avdo, because he didn't let them attack the Serb villages. It is their right to live in their homes. We don't want their homes, but we were not letting them have ours. And Avdo didn't let them leave the territory to maybe steal a cow or something which would have meant survival. Whether he was fully successful in that, I don't know, but he did his best to bring that about, and you know that perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. I apologise, but I am now really forced to show document D62, because of your answers. It's a document signed by your husband. This is a court of law. If you are saying to me you know perfectly well this or that, then I'll have to show you this document. This is a document of the BH Army drafted on 26th June 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 28th June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It was signed by your husband; we'll see that on the last page. Can we turn the page immediately so everyone can see. You will see his name in the signature block. It says "Commander, Colonel Avdo Palic." Let's go back to page 1, please. He's submitting a combat report, and he says in the first sentence: "Based on the Order of the Deputy Commander of the 28th Division Srebrenica, Major Ramiz Becirevic, strictly confidential number," so-and-so, "dated 20 June 1995," which means June 1995, "on measures to be taken for the execution of sabotage actions aimed at afflicting losses upon the aggressor in terms of troops and equipment, and in general, at turning Chetnik forces away from Sarajevo. "Upon receipt of the orders given me by brigade commanders, Major Zulfo Tursunovic and Ibrahim Mandzic, and by the assistant for intelligence in the division, Captain Ekrem Salihovic, I reviewed the overall situation with respect to this kind of combat action, and based on earlier instructions issued to the Chief of Staff Major Ramo Cardakovic by the Chief of General Staff Brigadier General Enver Hadzihasanovic, I decided, together with Tursunovic and Mandzic, to proceed as follows." And then in paragraph two it reads: "Form a number of sabotage groups." And I'll refrain from reading on to save time. You'll see that nine sabotage groups were formed, and they are given exact tasks, and their targets are mentioned, such as Zljebovi and so on, Rijeka, the former administrative building of Romanija Sokolac, communication centre Solilo, the Chetnik fortification and observation post, Crna Rijeka where the Main Staff was and so on. And now if we look at the last paragraph on this page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The following page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- "some 90 Chetniks were killed, dozens were taken prisoner and a significant quantity of infantry armaments were seized," and then he goes on to list what exactly. And then Velimir Mrdjan is mentioned, born in 1975.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the following page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have it on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And so on. And he requests additional instructions how to proceed, and he says that their own losses amount to two killed. And in the last but one paragraph he says, "By carrying out the sabotage actions the -- the Chetniks have strengthened their positions and are grouping in the areas of," so-and-so. My question is: Did your husband with this group of officers from the Operations Group or 28th Division, as it says, with Tursunovic and Mandzic and Salihovic, organise these nine sabotage groups and send them to conduct activities in VRS territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with all these details. I don't know what they did and how. I remember that they did have this one prisoner of war, Velimir Mrdjan. You are mentioning some places, but this is the territory of Zepa. At that time, Zepa territory was already being shelled from these positions where -- of the Chetnik forces. That's one thing. I don't want to go into the details if this happened and how because I cannot give information on that, but I do remember that prisoner. By the way, that prisoner was treated humanely. Whatever I cooked -- and he was wounded, and his soldiers left him behind, and now -- it's coming back to me now. Why did his comrades leave him behind? This was your sabotage action, and you left behind this soldier who was treated in Zepa, and then he was released in accordance with the Geneva Conventions which seem to have been unknown to you but Avdo knew them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you know that this document was taken prisoner with the communications documents where that group carried out its attack? He was taken to Zepa, he wasn't left where his workplace was to be treated there and he was released only after an agreement was signed and when the evacuation began, he was the first on the bus with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Take a look at the date. That all happened while you were already attacking Zepa. Take a look at the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I can see the date but --

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning in March we were shelled from Serb positions. During the last 10 to 15 days before the attack and before the fall of Srebrenica, those attacks were very, very intense. There was no peace in Zepa any more. You couldn't move around freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... This document, just put it on the record, is from the 28th of June, 1995. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there food in Zepa one month before combat activities, on the 26th of June when your husband wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Are you doing that on purpose, playing with dates? It wasn't the 26th, it was the 28th of June. I don't know whether you do that on purpose or whether you're trying to confuse somebody. I myself am pretty tired now. There was food in Zepa after the arrival of UNPROFOR. There was food. The food in Zepa was distributed in accordance with needs. That means that all citizens received equal shares, and at the time, there was no hunger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You're correct, this was on the 28th of June. That's when your husband wrote this report. He sent his groups earlier. However, a moment ago, you said that they had to attack because there was no food. Wasn't this particular attack carried out regardless of the food situation?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is not about that. This is about combat activities of Serbian forces around Zepa that commenced in March 1995. Just before the fall of Srebrenica, at least 15 days before, we were not able to move around freely. This wasn't a protected area, safe zone any more. You were shelling, and people were dying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. I would like to take a look at D52, D5-2. This is a document originating from the BiH Army, the 2nd Corps command in Tuzla. It is dated the 8th of July, 1995, in Tuzla. This is information on combat results of the units and commands of the 28th Ground Army Division of the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army. My question is: Was your husband part of the 28th Division of the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that it was the East Bosnia Light Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us take a look at the first sentence where it says: "The soldiers of the 28th Ground Army Division located in Srebrenica and Zepa, although completely encircled and facing big problems relating to survival and the obligation to protect free territory, decided to contribute as much as possible to the fight against the aggressor and stepped up their activities deep in the PZT, temporarily occupied territory. An additional reason for the activities of the members of the 28th Division was to prevent enemy forces from sending additional troops to the Sarajevo theatre of operations from the area around Srebrenica and Zepa by causing losses, primarily the loss of manpower, which will force the aggressor to tie up troops in the wider area of Srebrenica and Zepa." My question is does this show that there was no attack on Zepa and Srebrenica, but the other way round, that the attacks were carried out from Srebrenica and Zepa? Does this document show us what I just define? A moment ago you told us that there was fighting between Muslim and Serb forces and that the Serb forces started the attack, and now we see that it's something different.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that you submitted to me here, and I am telling that you from March 1995 onwards, because I remember that time very well, that's when I gave birth to my second daughter, literally speaking from the day my second daughter was born, I spent all the time in the shelter. I remember that time very well. Shelling was going all the time. And then just before the fall of Srebrenica, it was very intense shelling. There was not -- you couldn't say it was a safe zone any more. The freedom of movement, we didn't have. Now, you submit us this document, and I on my part want to tell the Trial Chamber that the Serbian forces shelled Zepa and killed people there. Specifically, they killed Ziga Nesud, they killed Nemis Hodzic. These are just the names I happen to remember right now. So they were killing, shelling. They made incursions. Now you're talking here about the territories that belong to the territory of the Zepa municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic. Take a look at the first point in this document where it says: "60 Chetniks were liquidated and according to unconfirmed reports the aggressor suffered even greater losses and had many wounded." And then they list what they seized and then slightly below, it says: "In the village of Visnjica, large quantities of ammunition were seized, but the soldiers were exhausted and could not remove it, so the ammunition was destroyed, as were all the facilities that the aggressor could have used for military purposes." My question is did you hear that the whole of the village of Visnjica was burnt? Did you hear that on radio of Republika Srpska? And did we present this on the 8th of July, and was it signed by the commander, Delic?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me about things that are outside the bounds of my knowledge. I really know nothing about these details. You can keep talking about those villages until tomorrow if you want, but what I know and what I claim here is that Avdo's army never killed civilians. Soldiers, they killed and they were the soldiers that were attacking Zepa, that encircled Zepa, that kept positions around Zepa and continually shelled us. As for the civilians, Avdo's army never killed civilians with Avdo's knowledge. And you know that, if you want to admit it. I know that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must come to an end for today. We're at the end of the third session, and we have to adjourn. You may continue your cross-examination tomorrow. We will resume at 9.00 in Courtroom I. Ms. Palic, please be -- I would like to thank you that you were able to stand this examination, and the court usher will assist you after we have risen. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 28th day of April, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.
